=== 58481 Cholla Comments Fee Discussion.pdf ===
                                      PROJECT NO. 58481




     CHOLLA, INC. RESPONSE ADDRESSING STAFF FEE RECOMMENDATION

I. Introduction

       Cholla, Inc. (“Cholla”) submits these comments specifically addressing Commission

Staff’s recommendation that large load customers be required to post a $100,000 per megawatt

non-refundable fee as a condition of inclusion in interconnection studies.

       Cholla respectfully submits that this recommendation should be rejected.

       The Commission has already adopted a financial commitment framework in Project No.

58480 in connection with the 2026 Regional Transmission Plan (“RTP”) load forecast. That

adopted framework allows multiple methods of demonstrating financial commitment and ties those

methods to real interconnection activity and cost exposure.

       Staff’s proposal in this docket departs materially from that balanced approach. A flat, non-

refundable $100,000/MW fee is not indexed to actual interconnection costs, is not structured as

protective security, and creates economic incentives that distort responsible load ramp planning.

For these reasons, it is both poor policy and legally vulnerable.




                                                                                                 1
 II. The Commission’s Adopted Framework in Project No. 58480

       In Project No. 58480, the Commission adopted a financial commitment structure that

allows large loads to demonstrate seriousness through one of three mechanisms:

   1. Posting of $100,000 per MW of contracted peak demand;

   2. Purchasing or committing funds to long-lead interconnection equipment; or

   3. Paying CIAC reflecting expected direct interconnection costs.

       That structure contains two important safeguards.

       First, the $100,000/MW component functions as security, not a forfeiture. It is part of a

broader financial commitment framework tied to interconnection progress.

       Second, the alternatives explicitly tie financial commitment to real-world expenditures

— equipment purchases and CIAC payments — which are directly connected to actual

interconnection costs.

       The adopted structure therefore recognizes that financial commitment can be demonstrated

through meaningful economic exposure that reflects the realities of interconnection.

       Staff’s proposal in this docket removes those safeguards.




III. The Proposed $100,000/MW Non-Refundable Fee Is Structurally Defective

A. It Is Not Tied to Actual Interconnection Costs

       A flat, non-refundable $100,000/MW fee applies regardless of:




                                                                                              2
    •   Whether a project requires minimal upgrades;

   •   Whether facilities are reused;

   •   Whether network upgrades benefit multiple parties;

   •   Whether the project ultimately energizes without causing stranded costs.

       Interconnection costs vary dramatically based on location and system conditions. Some

projects require extensive direct-assigned facilities. Others interconnect near robust infrastructure

and impose minimal incremental cost.

       A uniform, non-refundable fee cannot reflect these differences.

       Under long-standing regulatory principles, financial requirements imposed by the

Commission should bear a rational relationship to the costs they are intended to address. When a

requirement is untethered from actual cost exposure, it ceases to function as protective security

and instead operates as a participation charge.

       The adopted structure in Project No. 58480 avoided this problem by allowing financial

commitment to be demonstrated through actual CIAC or long-lead equipment expenditures. Those

mechanisms are directly linked to real interconnection costs. Staff’s proposal in this docket is not.

B. It Converts Security Into a Forfeiture Mechanism

       Security is traditionally used to protect against stranded costs. If a project withdraws after

upgrades have been initiated, security can be applied to cover those costs. If facilities are reused

or costs are not incurred, security is returned.

       A non-refundable $100,000/MW fee reverses that logic. Even if:




                                                                                                   3
    •   No stranded costs occur;

   •   Facilities are reused;

   •   Or the project energizes successfully,

       the fee is permanently forfeited.

       This structure effectively penalizes participation in the interconnection process rather than

protecting against cost exposure. That distinction matters. A regulatory requirement that functions

as a penalty rather than as cost protection must be carefully justified. Here, there is no demonstrated

connection between the $100,000/MW amount and specific stranded-cost risk.

C. It Creates Distorting Incentives for Load Ramp Timing

       Perhaps most importantly, a flat, non-refundable $100,000/MW fee distorts rational load

ramp planning.

       Under Staff’s proposal, the financial burden of requesting 500 MW in Year 1 is identical

to requesting 500 MW in Year 5. There is no differentiation based on when that capacity will

actually be energized.

       In practice, developers face strong economic pressure to:

   •   Maximize early-year capacity requests;

   •   Front-load megawatts into the first available study window;

   •   Seek the largest possible allocation of early capacity, even if transmission will not be ready.

       Cholla has firsthand experience with the opposite approach. At one of our sites, we

intentionally delayed a significant portion of planned capacity until after construction of a 765 kV



                                                                                                     4
 transmission expansion. That sequencing was selected because it would allow the system to

accommodate the load more efficiently and reduce stress on existing infrastructure.

       From a system planning standpoint, that was responsible.

       From a financial standpoint, however, delaying energization reduces project value due to

near-term revenue gaps. If a flat, non-refundable fee applies uniformly regardless of timing, the

rational response is to request as much power as possible in the earliest year available, even if that

timing does not reflect realistic transmission readiness.

       This incentive structure works directly against disciplined Batch Study planning. Accurate

load ramp timing is essential to modeling coordinated transmission solutions. A flat, non-

refundable fee encourages behavior that undermines that accuracy.




IV. The Legal Vulnerability of a Non-Refundable Flat Fee

       Regulatory requirements must be supported by a rational basis and must bear a reasonable

relationship to the objectives they are intended to serve. A requirement that is not grounded in cost

causation and that does not differentiate among materially different circumstances risks being

characterized as arbitrary and capricious.

       Here, the proposed $100,000/MW non-refundable fee:

   •   Is not calibrated to actual direct-assigned facility costs;

   •   Is not calibrated to anticipated network upgrade securitization;

   •   Is not linked to demonstrated stranded-cost exposure;




                                                                                                    5
    •   Does not adjust based on project timing or phasing;

   •   And is not supported by a record demonstrating that $100,000/MW approximates actual

       cost risk across projects.

       Without that linkage, the requirement appears to be a blunt threshold rather than a cost-

based safeguard. That makes it vulnerable to challenge as lacking a rational nexus to the statutory

objective of minimizing stranded infrastructure costs.

       By contrast, the structure adopted in Project No. 58480 directly ties financial commitment

to CIAC, long-lead equipment purchases, or posted security that is connected to interconnection

activity. That structure is far more defensible because it reflects real economic exposure.




V. A Better Path Forward

       Cholla respectfully submits that the Commission should:

   1. Reject the proposed $100,000/MW non-refundable fee;

   2. Adopt the financial commitment framework approved in Project No. 58480 for purposes

       of this rulemaking; and

   3. Consider incorporating a tapered security mechanism that differentiates between near-term

       and later-year capacity.

       A tapered structure — where security is higher for near-term energization and declines for

later-year capacity — would:

   •   Better align financial commitment with planning impact;



                                                                                                 6
 •   Encourage realistic ramp schedules;

•   Reduce incentives to front-load megawatts artificially;

•   And remain tied to actual interconnection cost exposure.

    Such an approach promotes discipline without imposing arbitrary forfeitures.




                                                                                   7
 VI. Conclusion

       Staff’s proposed $100,000/MW non-refundable fee is structurally unsound. It is not

calibrated to actual cost exposure, distorts load ramp behavior, and is legally vulnerable because it

lacks a rational nexus to stranded-cost protection.

       The Commission has already adopted a more balanced and defensible structure in Project

No. 58480. That framework — potentially enhanced with a tapered timing component similar to

the approach Cholla offered in its earlier filings — provides a superior path forward.

       The financial architecture adopted in this rulemaking will shape the development of tens

of thousands of megawatts of large load in ERCOT. It should be disciplined, cost-based, and

legally durable. The proposed non-refundable flat fee does not meet that standard.




                                                                          Respectfully submitted,
